1.2    Objectives and Strategies
The objectives of the Traffic Management Plan are to ensure:
  • The safety of the road workers.
  • All road users, including vulnerable road users, are safely guided around, through or past the work
    site.
  • The performance of the road network is not unduly impacted and the disruption and inconvenience to
    all road users are minimised for the duration of the works.
  • Impacts on users of the road reserve and adjacent properties and facilities are minimised.

In an effort to meet these objectives, the Traffic Management Plan will incorporate the following
strategies:
   • Providing a sufficient number of traffic lanes to accommodate vehicle volumes.
   • Ensuring delays are minimised.
   • Manage all road users including motorists, pedestrians, cyclists, people with disabilities and people
     using public transport.
   • To ensure all work activities are complete sequentially with minimal adverse impacts.
   • Provisions for work personnel to enter the work area in a safe manner and in accordance with safety
     procedures.
   • All entry and exit movements to and from traffic streams shall be in accordance with the requirements
     of safe working practices.

3.       RISK MANAGEMENT
The following details the preliminary assessment of site hazards likely to be encountered, the level of risk
associated with each, and the control proposed. Note that the risk level is the level of assessed risk
without the controls in place. The controls listed have been determined as being appropriate in reducing
the risk to a level that is acceptable.
The hierarchy of control has been utilised to ensure that the highest practicable level of protection and
safety is selected:
   • Elimination
   • Substitution
   • Isolation
   • Engineering
   • Administration
   • Personal Protection Equipment
In evaluating the options, a key consideration is whether the option takes traffic around, through or past
the worksite.

3.1      Risk Classification Tables
                            Table 2: Quality Measures of Consequence or Impact
 Level     Consequence                                        Description
                              • Mid-block hourly traffic flow per lane is equal to or less than the allowable
                                lane capacity detailed in AGTTM.
     1      Insignificant     • No impact to the performance of the network.
                              • Affected intersection leg operates at a Level of Service (LoS) of A or B.
                              • No property damage.
                              • Mid-block hourly traffic flow per lane is greater than the allowable road
                                capacity and less than 110% of the allowable road capacity as detailed in
                                AGTTM.
     2         Minor
                              • Minor impact to the performance of the network.
                              • Intersection performance operates at a Level of Service (LoS) of C.
                              • Minor property damage.
                              • Midblock hourly traffic flow per lane is equal to and greater than 110% and
                                less than 135% of allowable road capacity as detailed in AGTTM.
     3       Moderate         • Moderate impact to the performance of the network.
                              • Intersection performance operates at a Level of Service (LoS) of D.
                              • Moderate property damage.
                              • Midblock hourly traffic flow per lane is equal to and greater than 135% and
                                less than 170% of allowable road capacity as detailed in AGTTM.
     4         Major          • Major impact to the performance of the network.
                              • Intersection performance operates at a Level of Service (LoS) of E.
                              • Major property damage.
                              • Midblock hourly traffic flow per lane is equal to and greater than 170% of
                                allowable road capacity as detailed in AGTTM.
     5      Catastrophic      • Unacceptable impact to the performance of the network.
                              • Intersection performance operates at a Level of Service (LoS) of F.
                              • Total property damage.

                                                     Table 4: Quality Measures of Likelihood
   Level          Likelihood                                                   Description
                                          The event or hazard:
                     Almost
      A                                     • Is expected to occur in most circumstances;
                     Certain
                                            • Will probably occur with a frequency in excess of 10 times per year.
                                          The event or hazard:
      B                Likely               • Will probably occur in most circumstances;
                                            • Will probably occur with a frequency of between 1 and 10 times per year.
                                          The event or hazard:
                                            • Might occur at some time;
      C             Possible
                                            • Will probably occur with a frequency of 0.1 to 1 times per year (i.e. once in 1 to
                                              10 years).
                                          The event or hazard:
                                            • Could occur at some time;
      D             Unlikely
                                            • Will probably occur with a frequency of 0.02 to 0.1 times per year (i.e. once in
                                              10 to 50 years).
                                          The event or hazard:
                                            • May occur only in exceptional circumstances;
       E               Rare
                                            • Will probably occur with a frequency of less than 0.02 times per year (i.e. less
                                              than once in 50 years).



    Traffic Management Plan 0922-01531 Rev. 6                                                         OFFICIAL                                                                17 | P a g e
IMPORTANT NOTE: The likelihood of an event or hazard occurring shall first be assessed over the duration
of the activity (i.e. “period of exposure”). For risk assessment purposes, at which point the assessed
likelihood is to be proportioned for a “period of exposure” of one year.

Example: An activity has a duration of 6 weeks (i.e. “period of exposure” = 6 weeks). The event or hazard
being considered is assessed as likely to occur once every 20 times the activity occurs (i.e. likelihood or
frequency = 1 event/20 times activity occurs = 0.05 times per activity). Assessed annual likelihood or
frequency = 0.05 times per activity x 52 weeks/6 weeks = 0.4 times per year. Assessed likelihood =
Possible.

4.1 Traffic Assessment and Analysis
4.1.1 Traffic and Speed Data
The Traffic Management Assessor or Delivery Supervisor must refer to existing traffic and speed data for
the proposed work location to ensure that the proposed Traffic Management Setups are compatible and to
determine the required working times. A copy of recent traffic and speed data should be attached to the
Traffic Management Assessment or with any work-related documentation.
Refer to MRWA Traffic Map for current traffic volumes.

4.1.3   Temporary Speed Zones
Temporary speed limits will follow the guidance within Section 5.5 of AGTTM Part 3, table 5.5 Length of
temporary speed zone and the Main Roads Code of Practice. These details will vary depending on the
project, location, and stage of the works. The Traffic Management Assessor or Delivery Supervisor must
provide details of temporary speed zones, how speed will be managed at the site, dates, and times.

For afterhours work, the posted speed limit should be reinstated, and the site left clean and free of debris.
If this cannot be achieved, appropriate signage, temporary pavement markings and speed zones should be
considered. Any afterhours temporary speed zones must comply with standards and guidelines and may
need prior approval or notification to the relevant Road Infrastructure Manager.

Where the minimum or maximum length of temporary speed zones exceeds the recommendations in
AGTTM, a variation with RTM and Road Infrastructure Manager approval must be provided. Where the
posted speed of the road is equal to or Lower than 70km/h, the lowest speed reduction must be switched
with intermediate signage to ensure the speed reduction is placed at a distance of L3 from the Hazard

4.1.4   Existing Traffic signals
The Traffic Management Assessor or Delivery Supervisor will assess the impacts of proposed temporary
Traffic Management setups on existing signalised intersections. These details will vary depending on the
project, location, and stage of the works.

Where any of the following criteria is met, the 0922-01532-Complex Traffic Management Plan must be
used:
   • Alteration to the function of the traffic signals or sign display.
   • Closure of a traffic lane where:
         o Within a signalised intersection
         o Within 30m of the stop line on the approach
         o Within 30m of the adjacent stop line on the departure
   • Closure of any part of a signalised dedicated turning lane.

Refer to the Main Roads Signal Approval Policy for more details.

4.1.5   Impact on Adjoining Road Network
Traffic flow and network stability should be maintained wherever possible. The Traffic Management
Assessor or Delivery Supervisor must provide details and mitigation techniques for impacts on the
adjoining road network. The details will vary depending on the project, location, and stage of the works.
Where significant congestion or delays are predicted at the planning stage, prior Road Infrastructure
Manager and/or RTM approval may be required prior to the implementation of any Traffic Management
devices.


 Traffic Management Plan 0922-01531 Rev. 6              OFFICIAL                                49 | P a g e
If significant congestion or delays is to occur on-site, which is unacceptable, works must cease and traffic
control measures removed from the roadway or scaled back, where safe to do so. If any unsafe areas
remain, additional protection must be implemented in accordance with the appropriate aftercare drawing.
Once congestion eases, works can continue or alternatively, return to site for a later date and/or time.

4.1.6   End of Queue Treatment
The Traffic Management Assessor or Delivery Supervisor must assess end of queues and provide mitigating
treatments as per the details provided in the Main Roads Code of Practice. This should be provided as
supplementary information which accompanies the selected Traffic Guidance Schemes. The requirements
and details of traffic queueing varies dependant on the project, location, and stage of the works.

Where required, the following should be used as a guide for determining queue lengths, further
information is provided within AGTTM Part 3: Static Worksites Section 4.8 and Main Roads Code of Practice
Section 6.8.2. The following information is required to determine the estimated queue lengths:
    • The speed of traffic.
    • The road environment (vertical / horizontal curves, road surface, etc.).
    • The sight distance for road users to Traffic Control position and ‘Prepare to Stop’ signage.
    • Driver reaction times (generally 2.5 seconds)
    • The traffic volume (should consider peak traffic volumes at or near the location of works).
    • The traffic composition (large vehicles require extra stopping and extend queue lengths).
    • Work times and duration.
    • Expected time traffic will be stopped.
    • Worksite length
Once all of the above information has been gathered the expected queue length can be determined by
using the following steps:
    1. Determine the hourly traffic volume in the direction of travel at the time of the works (where
        volumes are not available, the assessor should attend site and count vehicles for a 5 minute
        period).
    2. Divide the hourly traffic volume by 60 to determine the vehicle expected every minute.
    3. Determine the length of time to the nearest minute that vehicles will be required to stop, this
        should include hold times for the work and travel time for opposing traffic direction to clear the
        road based on the length and speed of the worksite.
    4. Multiply this number by the vehicles expected per minute.
    5. Determine the types of vehicles that will be using the road and multiply its length by the number
        (including a 3m space between each vehicle).

                  Table 15: Approximate Vehicle Lengths MRWA Code of Practice Table 9
                     Vehicle Type                                           Approximate Length
                     Car                                                    5.5m
                     Truck / Bus                                            19m
                     Trucks (RAV 2 to 4)*                                   27.5m
                     Road Train / B-Double (RAV 5 to 7)*                    36.5m
                     Triple Road Train / Large Combination (RAV 9 & 10+)*   53.5m
*RAV classification assumes the worst-case length/combination. i.e 27.5m trucks may be used on RAV 2 to
7 however worst case from RAV 5 to 7 is 36.5m.
Refer to the Main Roads Code of Practice for how to apply the calculated end of queue with the
requirements for end of queue treatments. Where additional signage or devices are required for End of



 Traffic Management Plan 0922-01531 Rev. 6                      OFFICIAL                         50 | P a g e
Queue Treatments the details must be provided to the Traffic Management Implementor prior to the
works commencing.

4.1.7   Portable Traffic Control Devices
Portable Traffic Control Devices (PTCD) are required on all roads within the Main Roads Network with the
following exclusions:
    • At permanent traffic signals, based on a risk assessment.
    • Where the total cumulative time of the stop-slow activity over a 24-hour period is 5 minutes or less,
       based on a risk assessment.
    • Activities 5 to 15 minutes at a single location or multiple different work locations based on a
       documented risk assessment with the following;
           o A site specific Traffic Management Plan
           o A Traffic Guidance Schemes (with an authorised Traffic Management Plan) determined site
               suitable by a person with WTM/AWTM accreditation
    • Stop / slow permitted for TTM set up and pack down.
    • Emergency and Incident Management.
    • In the event of failure of the PTCD’s

Refer to the Main Roads Code of Practice Section 6.8.3 Portable Traffic Control Devices Page 50 Table 12
for examples of Traffic Control Scenarios that are mandatory to use PTCD’s.
On all other networks a PTCD should be considered however, it is accepted that it is not always practicable
to install such devices and a risk assessment should be provided prior to the works commencing. PTCDs on
all other networks must be used under the following conditions however, the above exclusions may still
apply:
     • Roads with a permanent speed limit of 90km/h or more and over 2,000vpd
     • Roads with a permanent speed limit of 70km/h or more and over 10,000vpd

Where roadside hazards or features prevent or alter the placement of PTCD’s this will need to be identified
and mitigated where possible, this should be identified in the planning stage. A PTCD must only be
replaced with a Traffic Controller where the risk has been assessed and endorsed by an RTM. A Variation
to the Standards will need to be provided for Road Infrastructure Manager endorsement.

Prior to the use of PTCDs a risk assessment should be provided which determines; duration of operation,
time of setup, mitigations in the event of failure, traffic volumes, location of device and traffic speed.
Refer to the Main Roads Code of Practice for the approved PTCDs for the use within the State of Western
Australia.



4.1.8   Speed Management
The management of speed is a crucial contributor to a safe worksite and the chance of crashes is reduced
at low traffic speeds. The Traffic Management Assessor or Delivery Supervisor must determine the
requirements of speed management prior to the implementation of any devices. Where traffic speed is
predicted to be high at the planning stage or where excessive speed is observed on site the following may
be used to mitigate speed:
    • Implementing temporary speed zones based on worker clearances and Temporary Traffic
        Management arrangements (traffic control).
    • Roadworks pilot vehicles.
    • Narrowing lane widths, chicanes and close spacing of delineation devices.


 Traffic Management Plan 0922-01531 Rev. 6             OFFICIAL                               51 | P a g e
   •    Rumble strips and/or temporary speed humps.
   •    Variable Message Signs (VMS) and electronic/variable speed limit signs.
   •    Additional Police enforcement.

Speed Feedback signage MUST be used when the following conditions are met as per the MRWA CoP
Section 6.16;
    •   Workers on foot are not protected by a road safety barrier; and
    •   Works conducted at the location for a duration of 8 hours or more; and
    •   Traffic volume of 15,000 vpd (AADT) or more; and
    •   There is a temporary speed reduction of 30 km/h or more

The speed feedback display does not have to be displayed at all times e.g. the display may be turned off and
the device used to gather speed data when trialling other speed control measures.


4.1.9    Excavations or Above Ground Hazards
Excavations require special consideration to ensure their structural integrity and minimise the risk of road
users losing control and driving into them. The Traffic Management Assessor or Delivery Supervisor must
consider the impact of longitudinal depressions and above ground road hazards adjacent to live traffic
lanes during the work and where left unattended prior to the installation of any devices. Where an
excavation may constitute a danger, it is required that:
    • The excavation is fully covered, fenced, or backfilled when the worksite is unattended.
    • The excavation is covered, fenced, or filled when work is completed.
    • Only approved skid resistant plating must be used to cover an excavation.
    • Fully enclose the excavation. Do not use barricades, traffic cones or plastic mesh fencing that is not
        supported by a solid frame.



Refer to the following table which shows the clearances between excavations, or any ground level hazard
associated with the excavation, and the nearest traffic lane, relative to speed and traffic volume:

4.2      Road Users
4.2.1    Pedestrians
Where impacts occur to pedestrian facilities which may increase the normal use of the road facilities by
people with disabilities and other vulnerable road users they must be mitigated as part of the Traffic
Management advice. Traffic Management Assessor or Delivery Supervisor must detail all pedestrian
treatments where significant impacts may occur. Pedestrian facilities include, but are not limited to, Bus /
train stations, hospitals, clinics, surgery’s, shopping centres, other retail businesses, churches, schools &
universities, parks, and other recreational areas / sporting premises. Minimum path widths to be
maintained as per the following table and requirements outlined in the Traffic Management Advice:
        Table 17: Width Requirements for Pedestrian Paths – Austroads Guide to Road Design Part 6A
              Situation                 Suggested Minimum                        Additional Comments
                                            Width (m)
         General low volume                   1.2*                 •     General minimum is 1.2m for most roads and streets.
                                                                          •   Clear width required for one wheelchair.
                                                               •       Not adequate for commercial or shopping environments.
       High pedestrian volumes                 2.4                      •   Generally at commercial and shopping areas.
    For two wheelchairs to pass**              1.8
   For people with other disabilities          1.0
*In constrained locations an absolute minimum of 1.0m should be provided. In these situations, path users
should be able to detect other path users with sufficient time to respond and take appropriate actions.
** 1.0m absolute minimum for a single wheelchair, may be provided for short distances. 1.5m absolute
minimum for one wheelchair and a pedestrian passing side by side.

Traffic Management should be provided where these locations are adjacent to site or where a footpath or
crossing has been closed due to the proposed works. This includes but is not limited to; additional Traffic
Controllers on site to render assistance to vulnerable road users, footpath closures with detours via
existing crossing points and additional ‘Pedestrian watch your step’ signage.

Consideration must be provided for the installation of temporary Traffic Management signage and devices
to not adversely impact existing facilities. Sign placements must not be placed on footpaths unless enough
room can be maintained to allow vulnerable road users to pass. Where this cannot be achieved, sign
placement may be extended as per the tolerances listed in AGTTM or additional provisions provided on
site.

Any planned works within the Perth Metropolitan area that require the closure of an existing path—
designated by the Department of Transport as a Primary Route—for a period of seven (7) days or more must
meet the following requirements:
   • Obtain Road Planned Intervention (RPI) approval prior to implementation.
   • Include a Traffic Guidance Scheme (TGS) outlining the proposed path detour and associated
       signage.
   • Be approved by a Roadworks Traffic Manager (RTM) who has conducted a site inspection of the
       entire detour route.
   • Undergo a compliance safety inspection of the proposed detour by an Advanced Worksite Traffic
       Manager (AWTM).

4.2.2     Cyclists
Where impacts occur to cyclists facilities which may increase the conflicts between cyclists and motorists
they must be mitigated as part of the Traffic Management advice. Traffic Management Assessor or
Delivery Supervisor must detail all cyclists treatments where significant impacts may occur.


 Traffic Management Plan 0922-01531 Rev. 6                  OFFICIAL                                          53 | P a g e
Cyclists facilities include, but are not limited to, on-road cyclists, principal shared paths and dedicated
cyclists lanes.

Traffic Management should be provided where these facilities are adjacent or within the site. This includes
but is not limited to; additional Traffic Controllers on site to render assistance to cyclists, footpath closures
with detours via existing crossing points and additional ‘Cyclists in Lane’ signage.

Consideration must be provided for the installation of temporary Traffic Management signage and devices
to not adversely impact existing facilities. Sign placements must not be placed on footpaths or dedicated
cyclists lanes unless enough room can be maintained to allow cyclists to pass. Where this cannot be
achieved, sign placement may be extended as per the tolerances listed in AGTTM or additional provisions
provided on site.

Refer to Section 4.2.1 for closures of existing paths for more than 7 days.

4.2.3    Public Transport
The Traffic Management Assessor or Delivery Supervisor must design/specify Traffic Management to
ensure no adverse impacts occur to the Public Transport Authority (PTA) network. These details will vary
depending on the project, location, and time of works. Where mitigating impacts to bus/train stops or
services cannot be achieved, the Delivery Supervisor must make suitable arrangements with the PTA and
their service providers. Suitable notification should be provided through the Notification of Roadworks,
with details of actual work dates and times.

4.2.4    Heavy and Oversized Vehicles and Loads
The Traffic Management Assessor or Delivery Supervisor must assess for impacts on the heavy and/or
oversized vehicles network. These details will vary depending on the project, location, and roads. Where
significant impacts occur to the network, Main Roads Heavy Vehicle Services must be notified and prior
approvals may be required. Notification should be provided through the Notification of Roadworks, with
details of actual work dates and times. Where detours are provided to a road within the Restricted Access
Vehicle (RAV) network, the selected roads for the detour must be equivalent or higher RAV classification.
Vehicle swept paths may be provided to determine whether heavy and/or oversized vehicles can pass
through or around the worksite.


4.2.5    Existing Parking Facilities
The Traffic Management Assessor or Delivery Supervisor must assess for impacts to existing on-road or
adjacent parking facilities within the worksite. Suitable letter drops to businesses or residents may be
conducted prior to the commencement of works to provide information of any closures to parking
facilities. Where possible, these facilities should be maintained, and Traffic Controllers may be provided on
site to manage vehicles through the worksite. Project Delivery Supervisor to liaise with Local Government
Authority on the closure of parking bays prior to the implementation of the works.

4.2.6    Access to Adjoining Properties/Business
The Traffic Management Assessor or Delivery Supervisor must assess for impacts to adjoining property and
business access within the worksite. Suitable letter drops and other forms of pre-communication may be
provided to warn residential and commercial premises of the potential impact of the works. Where
possible, facility access should be maintained, and Traffic Controllers may be provided on site to manage


 Traffic Management Plan 0922-01531 Rev. 6                OFFICIAL                                 54 | P a g e
vehicles through the worksite. Where facility access cannot be maintained, detours via adjacent accesses
or other mitigating procedures must be implemented to ensure no significant impacts occur.

4.2.7    Rail Crossings
The Traffic Management Assessor or Delivery Supervisor must determine the impacts to the rail crossing
and other facilities and provide suitable approvals and notification. Where using the Rail Approach (Traffic
Guidance Schemes TMC-RA), prior rail infrastructure notification and/or approval must be sought. Where
site specific constraints do not permit the safe application of the Traffic Guidance Schemes, then a site-
specific plan is to be prepared and approved by the Road Infrastructure Manager. Any requirements for a
Rail Safety Management Plan (RSMP) will be instructed by the rail infrastructure manager prior to the
implementation of any works. Table 3 of the Code of Practice provides distances from the railway level
crossings within which the Rail Authority shall be notified via a version of the ‘Notification of Road Works
Form’ in appendix ‘A’.
                     Table 18: Distance from Railway Level Crossing – MRWA CoP Table 3
                                   Speed Limit          Distance from Railway
                                     (km/h)                       (m)
                                         <70                       150
                                      70 to 90                     200
                                         >90                       300
Traffic Controllers should take special care at rail crossings as motorists will generally follow their
directions when differing from other signals or devices. Where a rail crossing exists within a section being
controlled by a Traffic Controller, a flag person with the relevant Track Access Permit should be stationed
at the traffic stop line of the railway crossing at least 3m from the nearest rail. Flag Person must be
equipped with a two-way radio and are to watch for trains, advising Traffic Controllers with enough time to
stop traffic before the train approaches.

Where the section of traffic control is to one side of the railway level crossing, but within the distances
above, the flag person stationed at the railway level crossing shall be stationed on the same side of the
crossing as the section under traffic control, at the stop line or at least 3m from the nearest rail. The flag
person must be equipped with a hand-held stop / slow sign that has the rear ‘slow’ side covered. The flag
person must ensure that vehicles do not queue through the rail level crossing by stopping motorists prior.

All personnel within the rail corridor must wear orange, fluorescent clothing as per the Safe working Rules
on all rail networks. Traffic Controllers operating stop/slow within the vicinity of rail crossing should have
the slow side of the bat covered to avoid conflicts with existing boom gates/barriers.
4.2.8    School Crossings
The Traffic Management Assessor or Delivery Supervisor must ensure that no significant impacts occur to
school crossings within the vicinity of the works. Where works are adjacent or near schools, they should
be planned where work hours are outside school pick up and drop off hours to avoid excessive congestion
and delays during the increase in traffic. The affected schools should be notified via the Notification of
Roadworks detailing actual work hours and dates.
Any aftercare arrangements are to ensure that the site does not interfere with normal day use of
pedestrian crossings, particularly crossings around schools. Facilities must be left without significant
hazards and surface condition at crossings must meet normal use expectations.

4.2.9    Special Events and Other Works
Prior notification including details of each work stage, dates and times must be provided to the Local
Government Authority or Road Infrastructure Manager prior to the commencement of works. Details


 Traffic Management Plan 0922-01531 Rev. 6               OFFICIAL                                55 | P a g e
should be entered into the Road Space Booking System and those responsible for the delivery of the works
must check for conflicts.

Conflicts to the worksite include but are not limited to; adjacent events causing unforeseen increases in
traffic or impacts to the worksite, adjacent worksite causing conflicting traffic management advice,
conflicting detours from other sites causing adverse public reactions from motorists becoming lost or
unforeseen increases in traffic through the site and heavy or oversized vehicles needing access through the
worksite.

Where significant issues are identified in the planning phase, the Traffic Management Assessor or Delivery
Supervisor must detail these impacts and mitigating procedures as part of the Traffic Management Advice.

4.2.10 Emergency Vehicle Access
The Traffic Management Assessor or Delivery Supervisor must ensure that emergency services have
continual access through or around the worksite during the proposed works. Personnel must be on-site to
render assistance to emergency services and significant delays should be avoided. Where significant issues
may occur on site, notification must be provided to emergency services prior the commencement of any
works. The Notification of Roadworks should be used to notify Emergency Services with details of work
nature, location, date and times, and any on-site contacts. Where required police communications may be
requested to render assistance to a site where significant speed occurs.

4.3      Night Works Provisions
The Traffic Management Assessor or Delivery Supervisor must detail the requirements for additional
lighting or night works provisions. In areas where there is no street lighting and Traffic Management
activities become high risk without proper illumination, additional lighting towers should be provided.

All Traffic Controllers and/or workers installing light towers for night works shall have suitable training
and/or qualification to undertake the work activity. These persons shall conduct a risk assessment prior to
operating any lighting tower, to consider potential environmental factors including but not limited to,
overhead power lines.

All signs used at night are to be Class 1 Retro-reflective material and delineation will be either retro-
reflective or be sufficiently illuminated. All personnel shall wear high visibility clothing suitable for night
works and traffic controllers must use night wands when directing traffic.

4.4      Road Safety Barriers
The proposed Traffic Management arrangements does not utilise temporary road safety barrier setups.
Where temporary road safety barrier setups are required, a site-specific Traffic Management Plan should
be provided with all required details. Where the works requires the removal or replacement of permanent
road safety barrier that is preventing potentially catastrophic outcome the 0922-01532-Complex Plan must
be used, refer to section 4.4 Road Safety Barriers of that plan.

4.5      Shadow Vehicles
The shadow vehicle provides close protection to the rear of work vehicles and workers on foot. The
shadow vehicle must be used to protect workers on foot where the below scenarios are met, and the road
has the following traffic volumes.
   • All work on roads with traffic volumes that exceed 15,000 vpd.
   • Night works on roads that exceed 2,000 vpd.


 Traffic Management Plan 0922-01531 Rev. 6                OFFICIAL                                  56 | P a g e
   •   Scenario 1 – Activities / works within a traffic lane (open or closed)
   •   Scenario 2 – Activities / works within 2m of the live traffic lane on roads with a permanent speed
       limit of 80km/h or more.
    • Scenario 3 – Implementing or removing traffic management on roads with a speed limit less than
       80km/h (refer scenario 2 for speeds greater than 80km/h).
A shadow vehicle must follow approximately 40m behind the works vehicle, unless otherwise stated in the
manufacturers shunt distance advice. This distance should be regularly monitored to ensure that the
shadow vehicle does not drive too close to the work activity, potentially causing vehicle to shunt into work
vehicles, or too far from the works activity, increasing the chance of vehicles entering in front of the
shadow vehicle lowering the level of protection.

A shadow vehicle may only be omitted subject to a site-specific risk assessment, refer to the below table

4.6      Consultation and Communication/Notification
4.6.1    Other Agencies
In accordance with the CoP., notification to all relevant agencies is required using the ‘Notification of Road
Works Form’ attached at Appendix ‘A’.

4.6.2 Public
A comprehensive public notification of the works and traffic management arrangements that will effect
journey times may be required. Additional notification requirements shall be actioned upon request by
impacted stakeholders and/or the Road Infrastructure Manager prior to the execution of these works
where required.

The below are pre-communication methods which may be utilised, but may not be required for all
projects:
   • Notice to Motorists in the Newspaper placed [1] two weeks in advance, [2] one week in advance
       and [3] at the commencement of works;
   • Letter drop to all residents and businesses within the traffic control zone one week ahead of the
       scheduled works; and,
   • VMS boards installed 5 days prior to the works.
   • Significant projects will require radio advertising.

4.7      Temporary Pavement Markings
Installation of temporary pavement markings may be required after each individual stage of works prior to
the application of the ultimate pavement marking in accordance with the following:
    • After profiling works, delineation of lanes shall be via temporary RRPMs.
    • On completion of asphalt works, delineation of lanes shall be by either ultimate pavement
        markings, temporary RRPMs or temporary painted pavement markings.
    • The installation of temporary RRPMs shall be at not less than 4m spacing and not greater than 12m
        spacing.




 Traffic Management Plan 0922-01531 Rev. 6                      OFFICIAL                                       60 | P a g e
Temporary line markings will consist of raised retro reflective markers. Temporary reflective pavement
markers will be of the type manufactured with butyl adhesive base that allows easy and quick placement
on the road surface.
The markers will be fitted with retro-reflective tape on either one or both sides and shall be 100mm wide
by 50mm high. The road surface is to have markers applied in accordance with the manufacturer’s
recommendations. Inspection of all temporary pavement markers are required daily and any loss or
displacement made good immediately.

4.8    Temporary Traffic Management Requirements
4.8.1 Short Term Low Impact Setups
4.8.1.1 Works on Road – Protected by Specialist Vehicles
This practice may be used where at minimum a single lane remains operational on a multi-lane road or the
works are on the shoulder and vehicles can be parked clear of the traffic lanes. Refer to AGTTM Part 5
Section 4.1 Work Protected by Specialist Vehicles and 0922-01531-STLI-001 and 002. The works must not
take longer than 1 shift in any one location.

This practice is best suited to the following tasks (does not include all tasks):
    • Placement and recovery of temporary signs and barriers
    • Mobile lane closures
    • Progressively moving operations on multi-lane roadways
    • Verge maintenance including grass mowing.
    • Slow moving or stationary vehicles operating on the roadway.
This practice may be used to create a temporary speed zone, which must be terminated using a vehicle
mounted speed restriction sign or VMB. A risk assessment must be provided to determine whether a
temporary speed zone is appropriate and for the selection of the appropriate speed.
Where the vehicles are fitted with illuminated flashing arrow signs, they must direct traffic to one side of
the vehicle where it is safe to do so. Where it is not safe to pass or overtake the work vehicle the
illuminated flashing arrow should display flashing corners.

The specialist vehicle may be a shadow vehicle on low speed and low volume roads where determined
appropriate by a risk assessment and must be fitted with a flashing arrow sign. In all other situations a
Truck Mounted Attenuator must be used to protect the proposed worksite, particularly on high speed and
high volume roads. Refer to Section 4.5.1of this TMP for more details on where a TMA is required.

Where a shadow vehicle is used a 20-40m buffer zone must be provided between the vehicle and start of
the worksite. Where a TMA is used a reference must be made to the manufacturing standards for the type
of TMA, generally a 40m buffer zone must be provided. Consideration should also be provided by the
Truck Mounted Attenuator driver for a lateral clearance to live traffic lanes to prevent the vehicle rolling
into adjacent lanes when impacted.

4.8.1.2 Works on Road – Work Between Gaps in Traffic
This practice may be used where works are within a traffic lane and are undertaken for only a short
duration between gaps of traffic. This work should be carried out where a single worker enters the road
with simple tools and materials accompanied by a lookout person. Refer to AGTTM Part 5 Section 4.2
Work Between Gaps in Traffic and 0922-01531-STLI-003. There is no duration restriction to this type of
works but is dependent on whether suitable gaps of traffic can be achieved.
This practice is best suited to the following tasks (does not include all tasks):
    • Removal of obstructions or debris
    • Retrieving tools/equipment from the traffic side of a vehicle
    • Traffic investigations
    • Visual inspections on foot
    • Pavement spotting and marking
    • Minor pothole repairs
    • Survey works
    • Setup or removal of temporary signs / devices.


 Traffic Management Plan 0922-01531 Rev. 6              OFFICIAL                                 62 | P a g e

4.8.1.4 Works on Road – Frequently Changing Work Area (in lane)
This practice may be used where the work area moves frequently between successive locations of a road.
This work can be within the traffic lane. Refer to AGTTM Part 5 Section 4.4 Frequently Changing Work Area
– In Lane and 0922-01531-STLI-005 to 008.
This practice is best suited to the following tasks (does not include all tasks):
    • Stormwater pit maintenance.

    • Street light maintenance.
    • Pavement maintenance, testing and repairs.
Where this work practice is on high speed / volume roads within the metropolitan area, a Truck Mounted
Attenuator (TMA) must be used. A TMA should be considered for all other scenarios and may be used as
an option following a risk assessment. Refer to Section 4.5.1 of this document for more details. The typical
Temporary Traffic Management requirements for frequently changing work area may include advanced
and intermediate warning sings, a shadow vehicle, a lookout person, works vehicles and a vehicle mounted
warning device.

selected when:
    • Works are in one lane of a multi-lane road, but the remaining lane(s) are open to traffic flow.

        traffic flow.
    • Where the works are in a low volume road and the presence of the work vehicle and workers
        results in traffic operating in shuttle flow.

               difficulty turning a grader around at the end of a 2km section, the section may be extended
               to the next available turning point but not more than 6km in totally length. Within this
               extended distance, advance warning signs must be repeated at 2km intervals.

4.8.2 Class 2 Mobile Convoys
This practice may be used where the works convoy is travelling greater than 20km/h below the permanent
speed limit (work vehicles travelling at 70km/h or less in a 100km/h speed zone or 40km/h in a 70km/h
speed zone) and there are no workers on foot. This work must be under a mobile convoy that cannot stop
in live traffic lanes and vehicles must be at least the size of a standard utility vehicle. Refer to AGTTM Part
4 Section 3.2.2 Class 2 and 0922-01531-MS2-001 to 019.
This practice is best suited to the following tasks (does not include all tasks):
     • Linemarking using ride-on plant, self-propelled towed or pushed.
     • Operation of pavement test vehicles.
     • Raised pavement marker installation
     • Pavement sweeping.
     • Pavement testing.
     • Road inspections.
     • Snow clearing/spreading grit.
     • Shoulder grading.
     • Vegetation control (mowing and spraying).
Scenarios provided in the TGS cover a single work vehicle slowly moving on the verge to mobile convoys
closing multiple lanes, involving shadow, tail, and advanced warning vehicles. The scenarios provide
separate mobile temporary speed zones depending on clearance between the work vehicle and live traffic
lanes. Distances between each vehicle in the mobile works convoy, excluding the shadow vehicle, are
shown in the table below:
      Table 44: AGTTM Part 4 Section 3.6 Table 3.1: Spacing Distance Between Vehicles in Mobile Works
                                  Speed (km/h)                     Distance (m)
                                     ≤ 45                            50
                                   46 – 55                           70
                                   56 – 65                           90
                                   66 – 75                           110
                                   76 – 85                           140
                                   86 – 95                           160
                                   96 – 105                          200
                                    > 106                            230

Any signs or devices required for the proposed works must be attached to the vehicles within the convoy.
Where works are being undertaken on two-way roads, signs or devices required must be displayed on both
ends of the vehicle to warn road users from the opposite direction. All vehicles within the mobile works
convoy must be fitted with a vehicle mounted warning device which must not be obscured during the
works.




 Traffic Management Plan 0922-01531 Rev. 6               OFFICIAL                                 74 | P a g e
The position of each vehicle in the mobile convoy must consider the impacts on vulnerable road users,
particularly cyclists. The below describes the different types of vehicles within a mobile works convoy:
4.8.2.1 The Lead Vehicle
The lead vehicle provides advanced warning for road users travelling in the opposite direction to a mobile
operation. Where there is poor visibility on the section of road used in the mobile convoy, the lead vehicle
should advance its position to achieve a clear view for approaching vehicles. If a lead vehicle and a
temporary speed zone are used, the lead vehicle must reinstate the posted speed limit. The lead vehicle is
required on the following scenarios:
    • Undivided two-way roads.
    • For ride-on linemarking activities.

4.8.2.2 The Works Vehicle
The work vehicle is responsible for carrying out the proposed work activity on or adjacent to the road. The
works vehicle and activity, where possible must minimise delays to traffic when in operation. When the
works operation requires more than one work vehicle in the convoy, they should be 40m apart as a
maximum. Where this is not possible, a separate mobile convoy must be provided for each works vehicle.
Examples of work vehicles include, but not limited to:
    • Large item of plant (road marking vehicles, snow plough and graders)
    • Traffic cone pick-up vehicles
    • Road survey vehicles
    • Mowing vehicles
    • Street cleaners
    • Temporary Traffic Management equipment vehicles.
    • Sweepers.

4.8.2.3 The Shadow Vehicle
The shadow vehicle provides close protection to the rear of work vehicles. A shadow vehicle must follow
approximately 40m behind the works vehicle, unless otherwise stated in the manufacturers shunt distance
advice. This distance should be regularly monitored to ensure that the shadow vehicle does not drive too
close to the work activity, potentially causing vehicle to shunt into work vehicles, or too far from the works
activity, increasing the chance of vehicles entering in front of the shadow vehicle lowering the level of
protection. Where the shadow vehicle is part of a mobile convoy the driver must always remain in the cab
of the vehicle. Refer to Section 4.5.1 of this document for more details on the use of shadow vehicles and
the requirements of Truck Mounted Attenuators (TMA).

4.8.2.4 The Advanced Warning Vehicle
The advanced warning vehicle provides advance warning to road users coming up behind mobile works
and diverting traffic past the worksite. A clear sight distance must be provided on approach to the
advanced warning vehicle. Typical signage on the advanced warning vehicle includes, but is not limited to:
    • Regulatory speed sign to provide speed decrease increments.
    • Advanced notification of the type of works or Temporary Traffic Management setups.
    • Lane status sign depicting the direction of closed lanes.

On sections of roads where the sight distance is reduced, the advanced warning vehicle must be stopped
prior to the obstruction until enough room is provided for the advanced warning distance. The driver of
the advanced warning vehicle must alert vehicles within the mobile convoy of any interruptions, hazards or
approaching danger.



 Traffic Management Plan 0922-01531 Rev. 6              OFFICIAL                                 75 | P a g e
Where possible, the advanced warning vehicle should be positioned on the far left or far right, depending
on the side where the works occur. The advanced warning vehicle should be positioned on the shoulder or
verge and not within live traffic lanes. Where this is not practicable, use of a Truck Mounted Attenuator
and positioning the advanced warning vehicle in the lane or a static setup should be considered.

4.8.3 Class 3 Mobile Convoys
This practice may be used where the works convoy involves workers on foot which requires the convoy to
travel significantly slower than the existing speed limit. This work must be under a mobile convoy that
cannot stop in live traffic lanes and small items of plant or works on foot. Refer to AGTTM Part 4 Section
3.2.3 Class 3 and 0922-01531-MS3-001 to 015.
This practice is best suited to the following tasks (does not include all tasks):
    • Linemarking using ride-on plant, self-propelled towed or pushed.
    • Raised pavement marker installations
    • Pedestrian type linemarking and pavement marker laying or removal where a shadow vehicle is
        used.
Scenarios provided in the TGS cover a single work vehicle and worker on foot on the verge to mobile
convoys closing a single to multiple lanes, involving shadow, tail, and advanced warning vehicles. The
scenarios provide separate mobile temporary speed zones depending on clearance between the work
vehicle, workers on foot and live traffic lanes. Distances between each vehicle in the mobile works convoy,
excluding the shadow vehicle, are shown in the table below:
     Table 45: AGTTM Part 4 Section 3.6 Table 3.1: Spacing Distance Between Vehicles in Mobile Works
                                  Speed (km/h)                   Distance (m)
                                    ≤ 45                          50
                                  46 – 55                         70
                                  56 – 65                         90
                                  66 – 75                         110
                                  76 – 85                         140
                                  86 – 95                         160
                                  96 – 105                        200
                                   > 106                          230

Any signs or devices required for the proposed works must be attached to the vehicles within the convoy.
Where works are being undertaken on two-way roads, signs or devices required must be displayed on both
ends of the vehicle to warn road users from the opposite direction. All vehicles within the mobile works
convoy must be fitted with a vehicle mounted warning device which must not be obscured during the
works.

The time taken for workers on foot to complete their tasks should be kept to an absolute minimum. All
workers must be provided with communication devices allowing them to communicate with vehicles
within convoy and receive notification of any approaching danger.




 Traffic Management Plan 0922-01531 Rev. 6             OFFICIAL                               76 | P a g e
The position of each vehicle in the mobile convoy must consider the impacts on vulnerable road users,
particularly cyclists. The below describes the different types of vehicles within a mobile works convoy:
4.8.3.1 The Lead Vehicle
The lead vehicle provided advanced warning for road users travelling in the opposite direction to a mobile
operation. Where there is poor visibility on the section of road used in the mobile convoy, the lead vehicle
should advance its position to achieve a clear view for approaching vehicles. If a lead vehicle and a
temporary speed zone are used, the lead vehicle must reinstate the posted speed limit. The lead vehicle is
required on the following scenarios:
    • Undivided two-way roads.
    • For ride-on linemarking activities.
    • When there are workers on foot or pedestrian type linemarking activities.

4.8.3.2 The Works Vehicle
The work vehicle is responsible for carrying out the proposed work activity or aiding workers on foot, on or
adjacent to the road. The works vehicle and activity, where possible must minimise delays to traffic when
in operation. Where the works involve workers on foot and there is no lead vehicle, the works vehicle
must reinstate the posted speed limit. The works vehicle is not designed to protect workers on foot.
Examples of work vehicles include, but not limited to:
    • Large item of plant (road marking vehicles, snow plough and graders)
    • Traffic cone pick-up vehicles
    • Road survey vehicles
    • Mowing vehicles
    • Street cleaners
    • Temporary Traffic Management equipment vehicles.
    • Sweepers.

4.8.3.3 The Shadow Vehicle
The shadow vehicle provides close protection to the rear of workers on foot or the work vehicles. A
shadow vehicle must follow approximately 40m behind workers on foot or the works vehicle, unless
otherwise stated in the manufacturers shunt distance advice. This distance should be regularly monitored
to ensure that the shadow vehicle does not drive too close to the work activity, potentially causing vehicle
to shunt into workers or plant, or too far from the works activity, increasing the chance of vehicles entering
in front of the shadow vehicle lowering the level of protection. Where the shadow vehicle is part of a
mobile convoy the driver must always remain in the cab of the vehicle. Refer to Section 4.5.1 of this
document for more details on the use of shadow vehicles and the requirements of Truck Mounted
Attenuators (TMA).

4.8.3.4 The Advanced Warning Vehicle
The advanced warning vehicle provides advance warning to road users coming up behind mobile works
and diverting traffic past the worksite. A clear sight distance must be provided on approach to the
advanced warning vehicle. Typical signage on the advanced warning vehicle includes, but is not limited to:
    • Regulatory speed sign to provide speed decrease increments.
    • Advanced notification of the type of works or Temporary Traffic Management setups.
    • Lane status sign depicting the direction of closed lanes.
    • Advanced notification of workers on foot close to live traffic lanes.




 Traffic Management Plan 0922-01531 Rev. 6              OFFICIAL                                77 | P a g e
On sections of roads where the sight distance is reduced, the advanced warning vehicle must be stopped
prior to the obstruction until enough room is provided for the advanced warning distance. The driver of
the advanced warning vehicle must alert workers and vehicles within the mobile convoy of any
interruptions, hazards or approaching danger.

Where possible, the advanced warning vehicle should be positioned on the far left or far right, depending
on the side where the works occur. The advanced warning vehicle should be positioned on the shoulder or
verge and not within live traffic lanes. Where this is not practicable, use of a Truck Mounted Attenuator
and positioning the advanced warning vehicle in the lane or a static setup should be considered.




 Traffic Management Plan 0922-01531 Rev. 6            OFFICIAL                              78 | P a g e
5.       SITE ASSESSMENT
5.1      Provision to Address Environmental Conditions
5.1.1.1 Adverse Weather
The weather may influence the effectiveness of the traffic control detailed in the Traffic Management
Advice and Traffic Guidance Schemes. Where significant impacts occur on site the following contingency
plans should be used.
Note: any adjustments to the plan outside the tolerances provided in AGTTM shall be risk assessed and
approved by someone holding a WTM or AWTM accreditation. Major changes will require Road
Infrastructure Manager approval.

5.1.1.2 Rain
In the event of rain, Traffic controllers must perform an on-site assessment and sign spacing and tapers
may require extending by 25% to account for increased stopping distances. Placement of “Slippery When
Wet” signs as required and all changes recorded in the daily diary.

Where rain occurs, Traffic Controllers shall audit the site. Where signs and / or devices are not clearly
visible, Traffic Controllers shall adjust signage to improve visibility or if necessary, provide additional
signage and delineation. If the wet surfaces are affecting the stopping distance, Traffic Controllers shall
adjust spacing between signs to provide increased reaction time for drivers. In cases where it is determined
that the rain is heavy and the risk unacceptable; all work shall cease until rain has cleared. The daily diary is
to capture all the changes made by the traffic controllers.

5.1.1.3 Floods
Should works be affected by flooding to the extent that the worksite becomes impassable or risk is
considered unacceptable, all work shall cease immediately and Traffic Controllers (and other personnel if
necessary) shall be deployed immediately to close the site and direct traffic around the flooded area
(under the direction of the Delivery Supervisor or traffic manager). Emergency services and the Road
Infrastructure Manager shall be notified immediately and Traffic Controllers shall remain onsite until
emergency services and the Road Infrastructure Manager personnel arrive and take control of the site.

5.1.1.4 Other Adverse Weather (strong winds, thunder storms, etc.)
Where strong or damaging winds may impact signage placement, signs are to be weighted to ensure they
do not fall over. Regular site checks to be conducted to ensure all signage integrity. Where significant
impacts are expected prior to the works commencing, the works should be delayed or suspended.

5.1.2    Sun Glare
Where sun glare is adversely affecting a driver’s ability to sight signs and / or traffic control devices, Traffic
Controllers shall adjust sign locations and provide additional delineation and traffic control devices
necessary to address the risk from glare. Additionally, in the event that sunrise and sunset causes glare,
traffic controllers will assist in maintaining low traffic speeds. The daily diary is to capture all the changes
made by the traffic controllers.




 Traffic Management Plan 0922-01531 Rev. 6                 OFFICIAL                                  79 | P a g e
5.1.3      Fog/Dust/Smoke
Where fog, dust or smoke is identified as adversely affecting a driver’s ability to sight signage and / or
traffic control devices, sign locations may need to be adjusted and additional delineation and/or traffic
control devices provided to address the risk. All changes are to be noted in the daily diary.

Should works be affected by fog, dust or smoke to the extent that risk is considered unacceptable, all work
shall cease immediately and Traffic Controllers (and other personnel if necessary) shall be deployed
immediately to close the site.

5.1.4      Road Geometry, Terrain, Vegetation and Structures
The Traffic Management Assessor or Delivery Supervisor must ensure that the Traffic Guidance Schemes
and advice provided accommodates geometric design of the road on approach, through and departing the
worksite. This should include roadside furniture, curves, bends, crests, through terrain, vegetation and
structures.

Should the sight distance of traffic management devices, the traffic management personnel on site be
affected, adjustments as necessary may be made and recorded in the daily diary. Where the adjustments
exceed those given in section 7.3.2 of this Traffic Management Plan, an accredited AWTM person is
required to approve the changes prior to work commencing.

The following requirements from Section 6.17.1 of the MRWA Code of Practice must be adhered to:

      •   Merge tapers should not start or end:
             o Within 50 metres of the controlled leg of an intersection (both approach and departure
                 sides) on a Category 2 road.
                     ▪ If site constraints make it unavoidable to place a taper within this zone, a generic risk
                         assessment has been included in this TMP. However, this option should only be
                         considered after all other alternatives have been exhausted.
             o Within 100 metres of an intersection (both approach and departure sides) located on a
                 ramp to/from a Category 3 road.
             o Within 100 metres of a ramp (on or off) on a Category 3 road.
      •   Merge tapers on an uncontrolled leg of an intersection on a Category 2 road should not start or end
          within 50 metres of the intersection (both approach and departure sides).
             o If site constraints require a taper within this distance, a risk assessment has been provided in
                 this TMP. This must only be used after all other alternatives have been considered.
      •   Merge tapers must not be implemented through or across an intersection or ramp.

5.2        Existing Traffic and Advertising Signage
Covering is required for existing traffic signs that are contrary to the temporary traffic control and are
within the traffic control zone. These include but are not limited to the posted speed limit signs within the
section of road under temporary speed restriction. The Traffic Management Assessor or Delivery
Supervisor should identify signs to be covered within the temporary traffic management setup. Where
signs are identified on site as contradictory by the Traffic Management Implementor any adjustments
made must be noted in the Daily Dairy.

Existing advertisement signs must not distract from the temporary traffic management setups.




 Traffic Management Plan 0922-01531 Rev. 6                OFFICIAL                                80 | P a g e
6.       SAFETY PLAN
6.1      Occupational Safety and Health
All persons and organisations undertaking these works or using the roadwork site have a duty of care
under statute and common law to themselves, their employees, and all site users, lawfully using the site, to
take all reasonable measures to prevent accident or injury.

This Traffic Management Plan forms part of the overall project Safety Management Plan and provides
details on how all road users considered likely to pass through, past, or around the worksite safely and
efficiently will be managed for the full duration of the site occupancy and works.

6.2      Roles and Responsibilities
6.2.1    Responsibilities
The Site Supervisor has the ultimate responsibility to ensure that the Traffic Management Plan and
associated Traffic Guidance Schemes, is installed correctly for the prevention of injury and property
damage to employees, contractors, sub-contractors, road-users, and all members of the public. The Site
Supervisor, through the pre-start meeting, shall communication to all staff the need to mitigate risks and
hazards on the worksite, including maintaining escape routes from traffic and plant at all times.

The Delivery Supervisor will ensure all site personnel are fully aware of their responsibilities, and that
traffic controllers are appropriately trained and accredited. The Delivery Supervisor must ensure that
sufficient controllers are available to ensure appropriate breaks are taken.

The works must not commence or continue until all signs, devices and barricades are in place and
operational in accordance with the requirements of this Traffic Management Plan and associated Traffic
Guidance Schemes.

Traffic Management personnel must ensure that the number, type and location of signs, devices and
barricades are as per the relevant Traffic Guidance Schemes, Traffic Management Advice, Main Roads WA
Code of Practice, AGTTM and AS 1742.3. Should a situation arise that is not covered by this Traffic
Management Plan, the Road Infrastructure Manager shall be notified.

The Road Infrastructure Manager may direct erection, relocation or removal of signs or devices, which in
the opinion of the Road Infrastructure Manager, are not in accordance with this Traffic Management Plan
and do not provide sufficient safety for road users. If not complied to, the Road Infrastructure Manager
may arrange for erection, relocation or removal by others at the cost of the Contractor.

6.2.2.1 Road Infrastructure Manager
The Road Infrastructure Manager has a statutory duty to ensure so far as reasonably practicable the safe
and efficient operation of the road network under their authority. Refer to AGTTM Part 8 Processes and
Procedures Table 5.3 for the required responsibilities of the Road Infrastructure Manager.

6.2.2.2 Traffic Management Designer
The Traffic Management Designer is responsible for the following:
    • Designing and drafting the Traffic Management Plan, including all associated Traffic Guidance
        Schemes, to be compliant with legislative requirements.
    • Ensuring that the scenarios provided will protect both workers and public.
    • Developing the Traffic Management Plan and associated Traffic Guidance Schemes to
        accommodate changes to the scope or updates to the standards.




 Traffic Management Plan 0922-01531 Rev. 6                OFFICIAL                                 82 | P a g e
6.2.2.3 Traffic Management Assessor
The Traffic Management Assessor is responsible for providing any additional Traffic Management related
advice for the proposed works. The Traffic Management Assessor should work closely with, may be in the
same role as or may be engaged by the Delivery Supervisor to ensure the safe and timely delivery of the
works. This may include but is not limited to:
    • Selecting appropriate Traffic Guidance Schemes to be used to protect works.
    • Site Specific Traffic Management sign and device requirements.
    • Proposed times and hours of works to comply with traffic analysis.
    • Traffic volumes and traffic data analysis.
    • Use and requirements of additional Traffic Management devices such as PTCDs or TMAs.
    • Additional Risk Assessment provided at the planning stage.
    • Traffic Management staging requirements.
    • Pedestrian / Cyclists management.
    • Aftercare arrangements.
    • Requirements for Notification of Roadworks.

6.2.2.4 Delivery Supervisor
The Delivery Supervisor must have the ultimate responsibility to ensure that the Traffic Management Plan,
including all associated Traffic Guidance Schemes have been selected to cover the scope of the works and
identifies all measures required for safe delivery of the works. This role may be completed by multiple
individuals, including members from the Road Infrastructure Manager role to ensure the delivery of the
works. The Delivery Supervisor is responsible for the following:
    • Ensuring they have the appropriate authorisation from the Road Infrastructure Manager.
    • Ensuring they have an approved and accepted Traffic Management Plan, including all associated
        Traffic Guidance Schemes before commencing works.
    • Hold a BWTM Accreditation if selecting a TGS for Implementation
    • Ensuring that the selected Traffic Guidance Schemes cover the proposed worksite conditions.
    • Ensuring that there is an approved copy of the Traffic Management Plan, including all associated
        Traffic Guidance Schemes available on site (digital copies are accepted).
    • Ensuring any Temporary Speed Zones have appropriate approval.
    • Obtaining approval and timings for occupation of the worksite from the Road Infrastructure
        Manager, prior to commencing work.
    • Operating in terms of the applicable traffic regulations.
    • Ensuring that the Traffic Management and work teams are supported in matters of safety.
    • Ensuring that all Traffic Management and work personnel are suitably trained and qualified for the
        works.
    • Ensure that a suitable number of work personnel are in place to apply, maintain and remove the
        Traffic Management devices and to facilitate the works.
    • Arranging and recording details of inspections of Temporary Traffic Management measures.
    • Arranging for the publication of approved notices in appropriate media as specified by the Traffic
        Management advice.
    • Ensure suitable communication and consultation with the affected stakeholders is always
        maintained.
    • Review feedback from field inspections, worksite personnel and members of the public, and take
        action to amend the traffic control measures as appropriate following approval from the Road
        Infrastructure Manager.




 Traffic Management Plan 0922-01531 Rev. 6            OFFICIAL                              83 | P a g e
6.2.2.4.1      Roadworks Traffic Manager
The Roadworks Traffic Manager is responsible for ensuring that plans involving ‘Complex Traffic
Arrangements’, particularly in the Metropolitan Region and as defined in the Main Roads Code of Practice,
will be reviewed and endorsed prior to works commencing. The Roadworks Traffic Management must
ensure the following:
    • Receive the fully compiled Traffic Management Plan, including all associated Traffic Guidance
        Schemes and any further Traffic Management documentation or advice from the Delivery
        Supervisor.
    • Recommend any changes/additions to the proposed Traffic Management documentation and
        setups to the Delivery Supervisor.
    • Send the signed and endorsed Traffic Management documentation, once reviewed to the Delivery
        Supervisor.
    • Be contacted where on-site changes are required that are outside the scope of an AWTM risk
        assessment using the risk assessment matrix provided in this Traffic Management Plan.
    • Endorse on-site changes where required, all changes are to be noted in the daily diary by the Traffic
        Management Supervisor and copies forward to the Roadworks Traffic Manager once the shift is
        complete.
    • Suspend/stop the works where the on-site changes are deemed dangerous or unfit for purpose.

6.2.2.5 Site Supervisor
The Site Supervisor is responsible for overseeing the day-to-day activities and the practical application of
the proposed Traffic Management staging. The Site Supervisor is responsible for the following:
    • Instruct workers on the relevant safety standards, including the correct wearing of high visibility
        safety vests and night-work safety requirements
    • Ensure traffic control measures are implemented and maintained as per the relevant/selected
        Traffic Guidance Scheme.
    • Undertake and submit the required inspection and evaluation reports to management.
    • Render assistance to road users and stakeholders when incidences arising out of the works affect
        the network performance or the safety of road users and workers.
    • Take appropriate action to correct unsafe conditions, including any necessary modification to
        selected Traffic Guidance Schemes with the scope of their qualification and as per the Main Roads
        Code of Practice.

6.2.2.6 Traffic Management Supervisor
The Traffic Management Supervisor is responsible for the practical application of the Traffic Management
devices and personnel in accordance with the appropriate Traffic Guidance Schemes, AGTTM, Main Roads
Code of Practice and AS 1742.3. The Traffic Management Supervisor is responsible for the following:
    • Prior to any implementation activities on site the Traffic Management Supervisor must execute all
        actions outlined in the Austroads Guide to Temporary Traffic Management Part 6, Field Staff –
        Implementation and Operations.
    • Ensuring the Traffic Management devices are set out in accordance with the Traffic Guidance
        Schemes, AGTTM and Main Roads Code of Practice.
    • Ensure that the quality and quantity of Traffic Management devices matches the relevant Traffic
        Guidance Scheme, Main Roads Code of Practice and AS 1742.3.
    • Have all relevant qualifications, including Worksite Traffic Management for complex Traffic
        Management arrangements.
    • Must be on site to manage variations, contingencies and emergencies and take overall
        responsibility for the implemented Traffic Management setups.


 Traffic Management Plan 0922-01531 Rev. 6              OFFICIAL                                84 | P a g e
      •   Where changes are required to complex Traffic Management arrangements, the Traffic
          Management Supervisor must risk assess those changes and record variations in the Daily Diary.
          Where an RTM is not consulted, all changes must be within the original scope and objectives of the
          proposed Traffic Guidance Schemes. All other changes must be endorsed by the RTM and must be
          authorised by the Road Infrastructure Manager.
      •   Ensure there is a copy of the approved Traffic Management Plan and all associated Traffic Guidance
          Schemes are available on site at all times.

6.2.2.7 Traffic Management Implementers, Traffic Control and Other TM Related Personnel
The Traffic Management Implementers and Other Traffic Management Related Personnel are responsible
for the implementation of Traffic Management signage and devices to ensure a safe and compliant
worksite. Traffic Controllers must be used to control road users to avoid conflict with plant, workers,
traffic and pedestrians, and to stop and direct traffic in emergencies. The roles are responsible for the
following:
    • Operate in accordance Austroads Guide to Temporary Traffic Management Part 6 – Field Staff and
         Part 7 – Traffic Controllers.
    • Have all relevant qualifications and licenses available on site as evidence of completion, including
         Basic Worksite Traffic Management and Traffic Control accreditations.
    • Take appropriate breaks as required in Austroads Guide to Temporary Traffic Management Part 6 –
         Field Staff, Part 7 – Traffic Controllers and/or the relevant WS&H Regulations.
    • Correctly wear high visibility vests, in addition to other protective equipment required (including
         night wands for night works).
    • Comply with the requirements of the Traffic Management Plan, including all associated Traffic
         Guidance Schemes.
    • Ensure no activity is undertaken that will endanger the safety of other workers or the public.
    • Enter and leave the site by approved routes and in accordance with safe work practices.
    • Take reasonable care for their own health and safety and of other persons.
    • Always comply with the requirements of the traffic rules.
    • Be aware of the general configuration of signs and devices and report a defect to the Traffic
         Management Supervisor.
    • Record all incidents and complaints at the worksite to the Traffic Management Supervisor and Site
         Supervisor, to be notified to the Delivery Supervisor or Road Infrastructure Manager as required.
    • At least one accredited person with Basic Worksite Traffic Management must remain on site with
         the responsibility of ensuring the traffic management devices are set out in accordance with the
         TMP.

6.3        Personal Protective Equipment
All personnel entering the work site shall correctly wear high visibility vests to AS/NZS 4602, in addition to
other protective equipment required on a site-by-site basis (e.g. protective footwear, eye protection,
helmet, sun protection, respiratory devices etc.) at all times whilst on the worksite.

6.4        Plant and Equipment
All plant and equipment at the workplace shall meet statutory requirements and have the required
registration, licences or certification where required. All mobile equipment shall be fitted with suitable
reversing alarms. All mobile plant and vehicles shall be fitted with a pair of rotating flashing yellow lamps
in accordance with AS1742.3 clause 4.14.1. All workers are aware of the safe work practice at the time of
the site induction.



 Traffic Management Plan 0922-01531 Rev. 6               OFFICIAL                                85 | P a g e
6.5     Trip Hazards
The worksite and its immediate surroundings shall be suitably protected and free of hazards, which could
result in tripping by cyclists or pedestrians. Hazards, which cannot be removed, shall be suitably protected
to prevent injury to road users, including those with sight impairment. Where level differences are
significant, suitable barriers, which preclude pedestrian access shall be used. Where works extend beyond
daylight hours and adjacent lighting is insufficient to illuminate hazards to cyclists or pedestrians,
appropriate temporary lighting shall be installed. To reduce the risk to workers the worksite will remain
tidy.

Below is a list of the current approved drawings, sorted in alphabetical order. Each TGS has been assigned
an implementation/selection requirement based on the complexity of the proposed TM. The below
headings define each implementation/selection requirement in further detail:

7.1.1 Independent Works Crew
These drawings may be implemented by an Independent Works Crew and may not require additional
Traffic Management Implementers. These scenarios may be selected by all other levels of qualification
outlined in this Traffic Management Plan.

7.1.2 TMI with BWTM
These drawings may be implemented by dedicated Traffic Management Implementers with Basic Worksite
Traffic Management Qualification. These scenarios may be selected and implemented by persons with
Basic Worksite Traffic Management, Worksite Traffic Management and Advanced Worksite Traffic
Management qualification but is not recommended for Individual Work Crews.

7.1.3 TMI with 3 Months Experience
These drawings may be implemented by Traffic Management Implementers with Basic Worksite Traffic
Management Qualification and a minimum of 3 months working experiencing installing signs and devices.
Due to the more complex nature of the setups, it is recommended for Traffic Management Implementers
with on-site experience. Alternatively, the works may be implemented/selected by an individual with a
Worksite Traffic Management or Advanced Worksite Traffic Management Qualification. These scenarios
must not be implemented by an Independent Work Crew.

7.1.4 Additional Planning & Approvals
These drawings require additional stakeholder approval prior to implementation. Due to the complex
nature of the setups, it is recommended that an individual with a Worksite Traffic Management or
Advanced Worksite Traffic Management qualification oversee the selection of these drawings. These
drawings should only be implemented by Traffic Management Implementers with on-site experience.
Special consideration must be provided to the implementation and running of these proposed Traffic
Management Setups.
